newsitem.title: USA: Johnson & Johnson U.S. stent monopoly under attack.
newsitem.headline: Johnson & Johnson U.S. stent monopoly under attack.

text.p: The near monopoly held by medical products giant Johnson & Johnson over the growing U.S. market for stents -- small metal tubes that shore up diseased blood vessels -- is under assault.
Leading the attack is Medtronic Inc, which is expected to get U.S. Food and Drug Administration marketing clearance for its rival Wiktor stent in the spring of 1997.
Not far behind are a host of companies, including Guidant Corp, all gunning for a bigger piece of a $1.2-billion worldwide stent market projected to hit $2.3 billion by 1999.

Introduced in 1994, stents have quickly become a vital part of the cardiologist's arsenal for treating heart disease, the leading U.S. killer. The tiny tubes are inserted inside cardiac blood vessels in conjunction with balloon angioplasty and left behind to support the vessels' walls from inside.
Analysts estimate that up to 65 percent of all cardiac interventional procedures will soon include stent placements.
The J&J Palmaz-Schatz stent is the world leader, but its dominance is more commanding in the United States than in Europe, where weaker patent laws have led to more competition.

J&J had global stent sales in 1995 of about $492 million, estimated Cowen & Co analyst Daniel Lemaitre. Of that total, about $260 million came from the United States, where the company controlled 96 percent of the national market because the Palmaz-Schatz has virtually no U.S. competition.
"In Europe, there are probably 25 stent companies," said Dain Bosworth medical devices analyst Sanjiv Arora. "J&J is definitely losing market share in Europe."
Whether rivals will be able to erode J&J's U.S. position will in part be determined by the outcome of a patent dispute with Cook Inc, scheduled for trial in March.

Privately held Cook has a Flex stent on the U.S. market, but its uses are limited, analysts said. Cook is in clinical trials with a GR2 stent, but faces allegations of patent infringment from J&J related to the Flex. The case "could ultimately determine whether the free-for-all playing out in Europe will be replicated in the U.S.," Lemaitre said.
A ruling against J&J could open the way for more competition, possibly leading to downward pressure on stent prices and profits, as is being felt in Europe, analysts said.

"It's not going to change suddenly in the U.S. It's going to play out over the next 12 to 24 months. But the European market is a good indication of what the U.S. market will look like," said Piper Jaffray medical devices analyst Arch Smith.

Besides Medtronic and Cook, rivals expected to enter the U.S. stent market over the next two years include Guidant; C.R. Bard Inc ; Arterial Vascular Engineering ; Boston Scientific Corp and others, analysts said.
